one_line_contribution: It applies a datamodels-style randomized-injection design plus a generalizability-theory variance decomposition to agent-memory items in order to measure, rather than assume, how much of an item's downstream utility is a stable item main effect versus item-by-query interaction, and then tests whether a curation decision made on that estimate transfers to held-out episodes against a bank-size-matched random-removal control.
closest_prior_work: Two things converge on it. (a) arXiv:2406.04606 ("Helpful or Harmful Data? Fine-tuning-free Shapley Attribution") already does the core reliability move — sign-instability of per-instance value scores under resampling — and the proposal's own split-half/sign-agreement analysis is that same test with a different object. The proposal's honest delta is the G-theory probe-budget derivation and the curation-transfer test, which is real but narrower than the framing ('item value is not an item property') implies. (b) The ICL demonstration-sensitivity literature (Lu et al. 2022 on prompt ordering, Zhao et al. 2021, and the influence-based selection papers the proposal cites) has made 'demonstration value is strongly context-dependent' close to received wisdom; a reviewer will ask what is surprising about item x query dominating for a demonstration-slot item. MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) threatens the framing rather than the measurement — it has already published the conclusion ('value is combinatorial, score against a package oracle') that the proposal's P-1 is designed to support, so the paper risks being read as the appendix that justifies a design choice someone else already shipped. It does not fully scoop, because MEMAUDIT reports no variance components, no budget derivation, and no held-out transfer test.
strongest_objection: The decisive experiment may have a ceiling below its own minimum detectable effect, which makes the headline null uninformative. The precheck gate only requires that the memory agent differ from the no-memory agent on 8% of instances *in either direction* — that is a churn gate, not an effect-size gate, and it is satisfied by a bank whose net accuracy contribution is zero. Phase 3 then removes 12 of 120 items and asks McNemar, whose stated MDE is ~3.8 points, to adjudicate P1 vs P2. If the entire full-bank-vs-no-memory net effect is ~1-2 points (which the track's own prior results suggest: zero fixes, six-to-seven breaks), then no 10% prune of that bank can plausibly move accuracy by 4 points, and P-4's predicted null is guaranteed by construction rather than by the instability of item value. P3 is offered as the ceiling bound, but if P3 - P0 is also inside the noise band, the paper cannot distinguish 'item value is unestimable' from 'this bank has no item-level headroom in this environment', and every downstream recommendation collapses. A second, independent objection compounds it: P-5 is entailed by P-3 through attenuation. If fewer than 10% of items have posteriors excluding zero, the shrunken posterior used as the correlation target is mostly noise, so |Spearman| < 0.25 for every proxy is an arithmetic consequence of the measurement's own unreliability and says nothing about whether A-MAC's or SAGE's signal is valid. Declaring a whole family of published signals invalid on that basis is the sentence an area chair will circle. Third, the estimand is mismatched to the target: effects are estimated marginal over a uniform k~U{1..6} draw from the retriever's top-20, but curation methods operate on items that will be injected by top-k retrieval. A small query-marginal main effect relative to item x query interaction is precisely the regime a retriever exists to exploit, so low reliability of the marginal quantity does not by itself indict conditional, retrieval-aware curation.
what_would_fix_it: (1) Replace the churn-based precheck with a headroom gate: before committing 8,800 transfer episodes, compute from Phase 1 the best achievable subset-selection gain (oracle prune evaluated in-sample on probe data) and pre-register that the transfer test only runs, and only carries the claim, if that oracle gain exceeds the 3.8-point MDE; otherwise re-scope to a bank or environment with measurable item-level headroom, or raise held-out n. (2) Estimate item effects under two injection distributions - the uniform top-20 probe and a deployment-matched top-k conditional - and report reliability separately for each, so the claim addresses the estimand curation methods actually use. (3) Break the entailment between P-3 and P-5 by reporting disattenuated correlations and an explicit reliability ceiling on the maximum attainable |Spearman| given the measured split-half reliability; state in advance that a proxy correlation below that ceiling is uninformative rather than a refutation of the proxy. (4) Fix identifiability: items only ever appear on queries where they reach the retriever's top-20, so item and query are confounded and the crossed p x i design that the G-coefficient formula assumes does not hold; add a fraction of probe episodes with injection drawn uniformly over the entire 120-item bank to restore connectedness, and report the variance decomposition on that connected subdesign. (5) Add k=0 to the held-out arms (see missing baseline). (6) With 120 items, split-half rho carries a +/-0.17 CI, which cannot separate 0.35 from 0.45; either enlarge the bank or state the reliability finding as an interval claim rather than a threshold claim.
missing_baseline: A no-memory (k=0) arm on the 800 paired held-out instances. The paper's constructive corollary is that the injection budget, not item identity, is the decision variable - and k=0 is the endpoint of that budget. Given the track's own prior finding that full-bank injection fixed zero items and broke six to seven, it is entirely possible that k=0 beats P0, P1, P4 and P9, which would make the whole item-value audit moot and reframe the paper. Running it only in a 150-instance precheck is not enough. Two lesser omissions a reviewer will also raise: a positive-selection arm (keep only the top-12 estimated items, bank size matched by a random-12 control) - pruning the bottom decile of a 120-item bank is the weakest possible test of whether the estimates carry signal, since it manipulates 10% of the bank at the tail where the estimates are noisiest; and prune-by-retrieval-frequency, which is the cheapest deployable heuristic and appears only as a Phase-4 correlation, never as a paid condition.
preprint_collision: Above the median for this kind of submission and clearly not fabricated boilerplate: it names nine-plus specific arXiv IDs, distinguishes targets from collisions, absorbs GovMem's signal as a proxy rather than dismissing it, and states the exact scenario that would gut the headline (a random-removal appendix ablation in a recent curation preprint). It also declares that only a single pass ran because a second was tool-blocked, which is the right disclosure. But it is thin in a way that matters for this particular paper: the search covered the memory-curation literature, not the paper's own methodological core. Generalizability theory and item-response theory have already been imported into LLM and NLG evaluation for exactly this purpose - decomposing rater/item/instance variance and deriving how many observations a reliable ranking needs (the IRT-for-benchmarks and tinyBenchmarks-adjacent line, and the LLM-as-judge reliability work) - and none of it appears anywhere in the Related Work or the collision check. The author flags 'generalizability theory applied to LLM evaluation' as an uncovered query and then proceeds as if the gap were harmless; it is the one gap that could turn the methodological contribution into a straightforward transfer of an existing recipe to a new object. The OpenReview 2026/2027 sweep is likewise missing, which matters when the direct targets are 2026 workshop-track papers whose authors are plausibly running the random-removal control right now. Verdict: no named collision, but novelty is established only against the curation literature, not against the measurement literature the paper's method comes from.
